sections.h2: Haverford Township housing at a glance
sections.html:
Haverford Township is an established inner suburb on Philadelphia's western edge, home to an estimated 50,997 people. About 87.4 percent of homes are owner-occupied, a typical home is valued at $466,400, and typical rent is $1,766. Most owners have been in their houses a long time, so sales here often follow a downsize, an inheritance or a house that has outlived its last update.

At these price levels, a roof, kitchen or electrical job adds up fast. Plenty of owners set the cost of getting a house market-ready against what an as-is sale would net, and that comparison is usually the starting point.

Name your neighborhood when you describe the house, because buyers search by it. Llanerch, Brookline, Beechwood, Oakmont, Manoa, Westgate Hills, Paddock Farms, Merwood, Bon Air and Chatham Park are all in common use, and many of the post-war tracts share the Havertown postal address. Transit helps listings too: the Norristown High Speed Line has seven stations inside the township.

The Building and Codes Department licenses rentals every year and inspects them before a tenant moves in. The unit is inspected again each time occupancy changes, so a buyer taking over a rented Haverford house should plan for that step.

Haverford Township rental housing license fees
ChargeAmount or rule
License fee$75 per dwelling unit
License periodMarch 1 to February 28 or 29
Due dateOn or before March 1
Late penalty$50, making $125 in total
Inspection or reinspection$50 per unit
Missed scheduled inspection$50
  • No more than three unrelated people may live in a rental house.
  • An owner-occupied unit may have only one roomer or boarder.
  • Student housing is allowed only as a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Renting counts as a business activity under the township's Business Privilege Tax, so a landlord also files a business tax return.

The license application needs a list of occupants and a copy of the signed lease. If you are selling a rental, give the buyer your current license and your inspection records, and tell them when the next inspection comes due.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has tenants
sections.html:
A rented house changes hands a little differently. The license runs on a March-to-February cycle and is due on or before March 1, so a sale that closes near that date is a good time to confirm the license is paid and the penalty has not been triggered. If your tenant is leaving, the township inspects the unit before the next occupant moves in, and the $50 inspection fee is yours or the buyer's depending on what the contract says.

Walk the rooms against the occupancy rules before you hand over records. Check the number of unrelated residents, any roomer or boarder arrangement, and whether any student housing was ever approved by the Zoning Hearing Board. A buyer who plans to keep renting will want the signed lease, the occupant list that went with the license application, and proof that your business tax return was filed.

If the buyer plans to move in, an owner-occupied unit follows simpler rules. Either way, put the license and inspection handover in writing so nothing slips between settlement and the next March 1.

Contractors working in the township must hold a township license. The department will not take a permit application without a signed contract, proof of insurance with workers compensation, and the cost estimate. Residential additions also need a plot plan showing building coverage and impervious surface.

Plumbing, generator, mechanical, electrical, roofing and siding, fences, sheds, rental housing licenses and contractor licenses can all be applied for online. If an earlier owner skipped a permit for a deck or addition, ask the department what its records show before you list, because a buyer's inspector may ask the same question.

Trees are regulated as well. A permit is required to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, and owners must keep private branches 12 feet above public walks and 14 feet above streets.

The department also has a contact for use and occupancy (U&O) inspections. Ask whether one applies to your sale, and what it costs, before you fix a closing date.

sections.h2: How are transfer tax and recording handled in Delaware County?
sections.html:
Your deed gets filed with the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds. Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent transfer tax on the property's value, and the recorder collects a local share that is divided among school districts and municipalities.

Property that passes to heirs by inheritance is exempt, which matters if you received the house and now plan to sell. For deeds accepted during the year that began July 1, 2026, the state's Delaware County valuation factor is 1.83. Your title company can give you the combined percentage and explain who pays which part under your contract.

The order of events is much the same on every route. First you settle on a price and sign a sales agreement. A title company then searches the record and totals whatever is owed against the house. Next come the township items: a use and occupancy inspection if one applies, any open permits to close out, and the rental license records if the house has tenants. The deed is signed at settlement and filed with the recorder, who collects the transfer tax.

Gather these before you list or ask for an offer:

  • Your rental license, lease and inspection records, if the house is rented.
  • Permit paperwork for any deck, addition, roof or electrical work.
  • Your mortgage payoff details and any lien information.
  • If you inherited the house, the estate paperwork showing who has authority to sign.

A call to the Building and Codes Department early in the process costs nothing and prevents surprises late in the sale.

sections.h2: Choosing how to sell a Haverford Township house
sections.html:
Owners here tend to pick one of three routes.

  • An agent listing can fetch the strongest price for a well-kept house, with showings and repair requests along the way.
  • Selling yourself avoids a commission and puts pricing and paperwork on your desk.
  • A cash offer takes the house in its present state, which suits an estate or a property that needs major work.

A cash sale skips showings, buyer financing and repair negotiations, and you pick the closing date. The trade is that the price reflects the house as it stands. At Haverford price levels the gap between an as-is offer and a renovated sale can be wide, so work out what you would keep on each path before you decide. Cash Home Buyers CA can give you a cash offer to set beside your other options.

faqs.q: Must a Haverford rental be inspected before sale?
faqs.a: The township inspects before a tenant moves in and again whenever occupancy changes, at $50 per unit. Keep your latest rental license and inspection record ready, and expect the buyer to plan for the next inspection.

faqs.q: Is an inherited Haverford house taxed on transfer?
faqs.a: State rules exempt property inherited with or without a will. Your later sale to a buyer is a new transfer and carries the state 1 percent plus any local share.

faqs.q: How many unrelated people can share a Haverford rental?
faqs.a: A rental house is capped at three unrelated residents. Student housing needs a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to take down a tree before selling in Haverford?
faqs.a: A permit is required to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, meaning one on public property or a street. Trees on private land follow different rules, so call the Building and Codes Department if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Which school district serves Haverford Township addresses?
faqs.a: The School District of Haverford Township does. It runs five elementary schools, one middle school and one high school, so name the elementary zone when you describe the house.
